fixes.explanation: An alliance is right, baker. The LORD says they form one, but against His will, heaping up sin upon sin (Isaiah 30:1). A plan can look smart on paper and still not be His.

No royal council in this verse, friend. The LORD says they form an alliance, but against His will (Isaiah 30:1). Verse 2 says they set out to go down to Egypt, to seek shelter under Pharaoh's protection (Isaiah 30:2).
That's right, baker. The LORD begins with “Woe to the rebellious children…” and says they are heaping up sin upon sin (Isaiah 30:1). That's a pile, not a slip.
Strength sounds like what they were hoping for, I bet. But the LORD says Pharaoh's protection will become their shame (Isaiah 30:3). The refuge of Egypt's shade will become their disgrace.

Gold isn't what they bring, friend. The LORD says the Egyptians bring neither help nor benefit, but only shame and disgrace (Isaiah 30:5). In the next verse, wealth and treasures are carried to a people of no profit to them (Isaiah 30:6).

That's it, baker. They carry their wealth on the backs of donkeys and their treasures on the humps of camels (Isaiah 30:6). The verse calls it a land of hardship and distress, of lioness and lion, of viper and flying serpent. And all of it goes to a people of no profit to them.

The verse has no ships and no Nile. It says they carry their wealth on the backs of donkeys and their treasures on the humps of camels (Isaiah 30:6). The land it names is a land of hardship and distress.

No carts and no oxen here, friend. The verse says they carry their wealth on the backs of donkeys and their treasures on the humps of camels (Isaiah 30:6). The loads sit on the animals' backs and humps.

Rahab Who Sits Still, yes. The passage says Egypt's help is futile and empty, so she is called Rahab Who Sits Still (Isaiah 30:7). So the name here belongs to Egypt. And the name fits help that just sits still.

That's a mighty name, but it isn't the one in this verse. The passage says Egypt's help is futile and empty, so she is called Rahab Who Sits Still (Isaiah 30:7). The name tells you what her help does, which is nothing. Sitting still isn't much of a rescue.

That name doesn't show up in this verse, baker. The passage says Egypt's help is futile and empty, so she is called Rahab Who Sits Still (Isaiah 30:7). It's not a scary name. It's a name about help that never gets up to help.

It reaches a lot further than one day. The text says it will be for the days to come, a witness forever and ever (Isaiah 30:8). The command is to write it on a tablet and inscribe it on a scroll. That's a message meant to last.

Right, baker. The writing is for the days to come, a witness forever and ever (Isaiah 30:8). It's written on a tablet and inscribed on a scroll. That's writing made for the days to come, not just one afternoon.
Ancient isn't the word they ask for, baker. They say, “Speak to us pleasant words; prophesy illusions.” (Isaiah 30:10). They asked for pleasant words and illusions, not the truth.

It's true, friend. The jar is shattered so that no fragment can be found, and not a shard will be large enough to scoop the coals from a hearth (Isaiah 30:14). It breaks in pieces like a potter's jar. Not one shard is big enough for that job.

That's closer to the plan they already made, baker. They carry wealth and treasures toward Egypt, and the LORD says Egypt brings neither help nor benefit (Isaiah 30:5-6). The Lord GOD says, “By repentance and rest you would be saved…” (Isaiah 30:15).

No walls or weapons are mentioned here, friend. The Lord GOD, the Holy One of Israel, says, “By repentance and rest you would be saved; your strength would lie in quiet confidence…” (Isaiah 30:15). It's a quiet way: repentance, rest and quiet confidence.

That would be good news for the horses, but it isn't what the text says. The people say, “We will ride swift horses…” but their pursuers will be faster (Isaiah 30:16). Their plan to outrun trouble doesn't work.

Weary isn't the word in this verse, friend. The people say, “We will ride swift horses,” but the text says their pursuers will be faster (Isaiah 30:16). Nobody is said to get tired. The ones chasing them are just quicker.
Just one, baker. A thousand will flee at the threat of one (Isaiah 30:17). That's a thousand people running from a single threat. Hard to picture.
Hidden isn't the word, baker. They're left alone like a pole on a mountaintop, like a banner on a hill (Isaiah 30:17). The picture is one pole or one banner standing by itself.
